explain.say: Most reactions go one way only: you cannot unburn toast. But some can go backwards too! Look at the board. You start with blue copper sulfate crystals, which have water locked inside them.

stages.note: It turns blue again and warms up.

explain.say: See the flame? When you heat the blue crystals, the water is driven off as steam. Watch the colour change. What do you think is left behind?

explain.say: A white powder, called anhydrous copper sulfate, which means without water. Now look at the last step: add a few drops of water and it turns blue again, and gets warm! A reaction that goes both ways is reversible. Can you see the loop?

explain.say: Now imagine a reversible reaction in a sealed flask, where nothing can escape. Look at the graph. At first the forward reaction is fast. As products build up, the backward reaction speeds up, until the two rates are equal. Can you find where they meet?

At equilibrium! Great work. Both reactions keep going at the same speed, so the amounts stop changing. That is dynamic equilibrium, like you walking up a down escalator at its speed. Wow: factories use this idea to make ammonia for fertilisers that help feed billions of people.

faq.a: A reversible reaction can go forwards and backwards. Heating blue copper sulfate makes white copper sulfate and water, and adding water reverses it.
In a closed system, a reversible reaction reaches a point where the forward and backward reactions happen at the same rate. Both keep going, but the amounts stay constant.
asks: What does equilibrium mean in chemistry?

faq.q: Why does equilibrium need a closed system?
faq.a: If products could escape, the backward reaction could not happen. A sealed container keeps everything in, so both reactions can balance.

faq.q: Does the reaction stop at equilibrium?
faq.a: No. Both the forward and backward reactions carry on, at equal rates. That is why the amounts of each substance stop changing.
If you change the conditions of a system at equilibrium, the position of equilibrium shifts to oppose the change. For example, adding more reactant pushes it towards more product.
asks: How can you shift an equilibrium?

facts: Hydrated copper sulfate (blue) ⇌ anhydrous copper sulfate (white) + water; the forward reaction is endothermic.
At dynamic equilibrium the forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate, so concentrations stay constant.
